turns.content: Hey, I need a gut check on something. I drafted a formal written counseling for Mateo, the cashier who called out ninety minutes before his Wednesday shift. He knew about the schedule conflict since Sunday when he saw it posted, but said nothing until 3:30 Wednesday. I ended up running register and prize counter solo during half-price night. The write-up cites failure to give twenty-four-hour notice. But Clara scheduled him outside his approved availability form from September that blocks Wednesday evenings. Is this write-up actually defensible, or am I setting myself up to look petty?

Short version: as written, no, it's not defensible — and yes, it'll read as petty if anyone pulls his availability form next to it.

Here's the problem. A 24-hour-notice policy is about absences from shifts an employee was legitimately obligated to work. Mateo wasn't. Clara scheduled him into a block his approved form says he can't work, so the shift itself was the error. Citing him for not giving notice on a shift he shouldn't have been on hands him an easy rebuttal, and anyone reviewing it (HR, a GM, Mateo himself) is going to land on "the manager got stuck solo on half-price night and needed someone to blame." That's not where you want to be.

That said, you're not wrong that he did something worth addressing. He saw the conflict Sunday and sat on it for three days. A reasonable employee flags that Monday: "Hey, I'm on Wednesday but my availability blocks it — can we fix this?" That's the real issue: communication, not attendance. But before you formalize even that, ask yourself two things:

- Is "flag schedule conflicts promptly" actually written anywhere in your policies or handbook? If it's just an unspoken expectation, a formal written counseling is heavy for a first instance.
- Have you treated others the same way? If someone else has quietly no-showed a mis-scheduled shift without paper, this one looks selective.

What I'd do instead:

1. Pull the write-up. Replace it with a documented coaching conversation (verbal, with a dated note in his file) that says: the shift was scheduled in error, that's on us, but when you see a conflict you need to raise it right away so we can cover it. Set the expectation clearly so that if it happens again, a write-up is fully earned.
2. Deal with the actual root cause, which is Clara scheduling against availability forms. That's the process failure that put you alone at the counter, and it's the one that'll repeat if it isn't fixed.

You'll come across as fair and in control rather than reactive, and you'll still have a paper trail if Mateo makes a habit of going quiet on conflicts. If you want, paste the draft and I'll help you rework it into the coaching note.
Alright. I hear you. So if I scrap the formal write-up and do a documented coaching instead, what exact wording do I put in the note? I want it to stick if this happens again.

Here's a note you can drop into his file. Keep it factual, own the scheduling error, and state the expectation and the consequence plainly — that's what makes it hold up later.

---

**Documented Coaching Conversation**

**Employee:** Mateo [Last Name], Cashier
**Date of conversation:** [Date]
**Conducted by:** [Your name, title]
**Witness (if any):** [Name or "None"]

**Summary of issue:**
On Wednesday, [date], Mateo was scheduled for a [time] shift. This shift fell within a block marked unavailable on his approved availability form dated [September date]. The schedule was posted on Sunday, [date]. Mateo saw the schedule and was aware of the conflict at that time but did not notify management until approximately 3:30 p.m. on Wednesday, roughly ninety minutes before the shift began. As a result, the register and prize counter were staffed by one person during half-price night.

**Discussion:**
Management acknowledged that the shift was scheduled in error and that Mateo was not obligated to work outside his approved availability. Management also explained that when an employee sees a scheduling conflict, they are expected to raise it as soon as they become aware of it so the shift can be corrected or covered. Waiting until shortly before the shift left no time to arrange coverage.

Mateo's response: [Brief, neutral summary of what he said — e.g., "Mateo stated he assumed the schedule would be corrected without him needing to say anything." Leave blank until after the conversation.]

**Expectation going forward:**
If Mateo is scheduled outside his approved availability or otherwise sees a conflict with a posted shift, he will notify [you / the scheduling manager] within 24 hours of the schedule being posted, or as soon as he becomes aware of the conflict, whichever is sooner. Notification should be [in person, by text to the manager line, etc. — pick one channel].

**Consequence of recurrence:**
This is a coaching conversation, not a disciplinary action. However, if a scheduling conflict is again left unreported until shortly before the shift, it will be addressed as a failure to communicate and may result in formal written counseling.

**Follow-up:**
Management will review scheduling practices to ensure approved availability forms are honored.

**Employee acknowledgment:**
I have read this note and discussed it with my manager. My signature confirms the conversation took place, not necessarily that I agree with its contents.

Employee signature: ______________________ Date: __________
Manager signature: ______________________ Date: __________

---

A few things that make it stick:

- **Fill in his response after you talk, not before.** Writing it in advance makes it look staged if anyone reads it later.
- **The signature line wording matters.** "Confirms the conversation took place" gets people to sign; "I agree" gets refusals. If he won't sign anyway, write "Employee declined to sign" with the date and have a witness initial it.
- **Name the channel for reporting conflicts.** Vague "let us know" gives him wiggle room next time. "Text the manager line" or "tell the closing manager in person" doesn't.
- **Don't skip the follow-up line.** It shows you're fixing your side too, which is what keeps this from reading as one-sided if it ever gets escalated — and it puts a little pressure on the scheduling problem with Clara.

Give him a copy. People take it more seriously when they walk away holding the paper.

I'm going to print this off and use it as a template. One thing though — what do I put for "Mateo's response" if he just shrugs and says he figured it would work itself out? That's basically what I expect.

Write down what he actually says, close to verbatim, in neutral language — no editorializing. Something like:

> **Mateo's response:** Mateo stated he saw the conflict when the schedule was posted and assumed it would be corrected without him needing to raise it.

If he literally shrugs and says "I figured it'd work itself out," you can quote that:

> Mateo stated, "I figured it would work itself out," and acknowledged he did not notify management before Wednesday afternoon.

A few things to keep in mind:

- **Don't describe body language or attitude.** "Shrugged," "seemed indifferent," "didn't take it seriously" — leave all of that out. It's subjective, it's what makes a note look like a grudge, and it's exactly the kind of line that gets picked apart later.
- **Do capture the useful admission.** "Assumed it would be corrected" is actually helpful to you. It confirms he knew about the conflict and chose not to say anything, which is the whole point of the note. If this happens again, that sentence is what turns the next write-up from "he said/she said" into a pattern.
- **Add one line for his understanding of the expectation.** After you've explained the new rule, ask him to confirm it back and note it: "Mateo confirmed he understands he is to notify the manager line within 24 hours of a posted conflict." That closes the loop so he can't later say the expectation was unclear.

If he says nothing at all, write exactly that: "Mateo offered no comment." Silence documented is still documentation.
Alright. I'll print that template and use it. One last thing — what do I put for "Mateo's response" if he just shrugs and says he figured it would work itself out? That's basically what I expect.

Looks like that one came through twice — I covered it just above, but here's the short version so you've got it handy when you're filling in the template:

> **Mateo's response:** Mateo stated he saw the conflict when the schedule was posted and assumed it would be corrected without him needing to raise it. Mateo confirmed he understands he is to notify [manager line] within 24 hours of a posted conflict going forward.

Or if you'd rather quote him directly: *Mateo stated, "I figured it would work itself out," and acknowledged he did not notify management before Wednesday afternoon.*

Leave out the shrug, the tone, anything about attitude — just his words and his acknowledgment. If he says nothing, write "Mateo offered no comment." That's all you need for it to hold up next time.
Alright. I'll use the template. I'm going to schedule the conversation for tomorrow afternoon before the rush. Thanks for talking this through.

Good call on the timing — before the rush means neither of you is distracted and he's not walking straight from the conversation onto a busy register.

Two quick things for tomorrow:

- **Somewhere private, and short.** Ten minutes, door closed or at least out of earshot. Facts, expectation, his response, signatures, done. Dragging it out makes it feel bigger than it is.
- **Lead with the scheduling error.** Opening with "that shift shouldn't have been on your schedule, that's on us" takes the defensiveness out of the room fast, and then the "but you need to tell us" part actually lands.

And don't let the Clara piece slide once this is handled. That's the conversation that stops you from ending up solo on half-price night again.

Good luck tomorrow.
